title: Ellington's first band and why Europe wants the old records
summary: Duke took ideas from his players' solos; Bigard says he never had a band like his first one and audiences in Europe want the old records, not the newer music.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: The guys gave him -- all the guys in the band gave him ideas, I mean, like if anybody stood up and took a solo, you know, and he heard something that he made playing that he liked, he'd tell them, "Play the solo. Play it again," until he got it. When he got it, then that's it. Then the next thing you know there's a tune coming out of it. That was Duke. He was clever, very clever. I won't take that away from him. The guy was clever.

But I -- Well, I say he should have given the guys credit for what they did. I mean, you know -- and he'll never -- he never would have a band like he had, his first band. Never. I don't care who he had in his band. You can tell from the old records -- I got a whole bunch of the old records -- and you hear the new records and you can forget them, and they got good men in the new records, I mean, but it's not the same band. And it's, like, people want to hear -- every time --
like he'd go to Europe, they want to hear what the old band did. They don't want to hear that new stuff he's trying to pull off, you know.
All those records that, those early records, they were immediately sold in Europe, weren't they?
Yeah, so that there was a demand for the band right away.
Sure. They didn't care for that new stuff he was playing down there.
